topics.label: Cocoon field assessment in Jordan and Lebanon
topics.description:
A 2019–2021 pilot project tested whether Cocoon planting reservoirs could improve tree establishment and water use compared with local traditional planting in Jordan and Lebanon. Menaqua Land Restoration worked with Jordan’s Ministry of Agriculture and the American University of Beirut, in cooperation with Land Life Company. The design compared planting seasons, species and watering treatments across contrasting sites, and also considered installation, management, monitoring and community participation.

The report found advantages in selected treatments, rather than a uniform survival benefit. At some sites differences were small or not significant; at harsh sites poor soils and low rainfall obscured any Cocoon effect. The authors suggest that lower supplied water in Jordan may partly reflect inefficient comparison irrigation; comparable supplies in Lebanon did not demonstrate the same water saving. Flood losses, emergency watering, damage and unequal follow-up limit interpretation. The existing Al Faisal and Maysara carob records provide specific trial detail. This is a descriptive project name based on the assessment, not a claim that MENAQUA is its official project title. The December-2021 report includes conclusions dated 11 January 2022; long-term outcomes are not established here.

topics.label: Al Faisal planting pilot
topics.description:
A planting pilot at Al Faisal in Jordan compared Cocoon reservoirs with local irrigation within the Jordan–Lebanon assessment. Olives and almonds were planted in May 2019, followed by source-described pine and carob in December. Monitoring assessed survival and height, using May 2020 observations for the reported comparisons.

Refilled Cocoons and irrigated controls gave similar olive survival; the unrefilled olive treatment performed worse. Surviving almond comparisons had poor survival, while the replanted pine comparison favoured Cocoons over its short follow-up. These results depend on species and treatment. Canal floods in December 2019 and January 2020 destroyed all carob plants and part of the almond and pine plantings. Pine replacement, extra watering, excluded data and combined scenarios prevent treating the original design as intact. Flood loss is not evidence of Cocoon failure for carob, and the report does not establish long-term establishment success. The assessment’s conclusions retain these limits rather than offering a universal planting or watering prescription.

topics.label: Maysara carob establishment trial
topics.description:
The carob component of the Maysara pilot tested Cocoon-assisted establishment against planting with irrigation in Jordan. Carob was planted in May 2019, shortly before an unusually hot, dry summer, in sandy soils with very poor water retention. Emergency watering refilled Cocoons twice and also altered the nominally unwatered comparison. The report therefore excluded the original no-refill and no-irrigation scenarios.

The May 2020 comparison reported only 1% survival for refilled Cocoon carob and 2% for irrigated carob, without a significant difference. The authors attributed poor performance chiefly to severe soil-water limitations; Cocoons did not overcome that constraint. January 2021 data were not used for this calculation because watering information was incomplete. Water totals include emergency supplies and are not event doses or recommended schedules. This topic remains specifically the spring carob trial: better fall pine/acacia results at Maysara involved other species, soil improvement and a shorter period without the summer, and must not be presented as a carob result or a controlled seasonal comparison.

topics.label: LIFE NIEBLAS
topics.description:
LIFE NIEBLAS is a restoration project launched in July 2020 in Gran Canaria and Portugal, coordinated by GESPLAN. It tested fog-water collection and planting methods to improve water access and habitat recovery in fire-affected landscapes. The manual covers project work between 2020 and 2024 and distinguishes planting targets from results. Traditional planting was compared with Cocoon, individual fog-water collectors and AFDS; the Portuguese sites tested Cocoon and individual collectors, without AFDS because of technical and logistical constraints.

In the table dated 26 July 2023, the innovative methods used less water per surviving tree than the traditional comparison. Cocoon survival was reported as 0.87 compared with 0.43 for traditional planting, with 57.4 versus 133.5 litres per surviving tree. These are project-specific ratios, not event doses, carob requirements or predictions for another site. Other method summaries use different populations and values and remain separate. Settlement, maintenance and support watering were still part of implementation. The manual’s wider water-saving estimate is control-based and has a retained arithmetic discrepancy; long-term ecological recovery or universal superiority is not established by this snapshot.

aspects.Watering evidence scope: These are LIFE NIEBLAS project choices and method examples, not universal plant requirements or species-specific carob recommendations.
aspects.Nursery example: Around 30 L for 100 plants twice weekly, an average calculated 0.3 L/plant/event (PDF 143).
aspects.Settlement example: 10–15 L/plant/event; Cocoon additionally receives a separate 20 L reservoir fill (PDF 143).
aspects.Maintenance examples: Traditional/Cocoon: 15 L/plant/event monthly July–September; IND: 10 L/plant/event on that schedule. SAD: about 15 L/plant/event, tank-full triggered, reported about every three weeks (PDF 143).
aspects.Support: Monitor weather and plant condition; a fixed quantity is not specified (PDF 143).
aspects.Storage estimate: About 40 L/plant for first-year summer provision, around 12.5 L/application, is a separate approximate storage-planning estimate, not a substitute for the method schedules (PDF 103–104).
